intro: Read the deck for the facts and these notes for the thinking. Each note under a slide explains why it matters, how to remember it and where people slip. Work the exercises in pencil, test yourself with the recall questions, and write your own notes in the margins beside mine.

sections.title: What Public Health Is
sections.big_idea: Public health asks why **these people** are ill and how to stop the next thousand, so it works on populations and mostly upstream.
in_plain_words: A clinician asks why this patient is ill. Public health asks why these people are ill, and acts through law, infrastructure, financing and surveillance, the organised efforts of society. The two are partners: a strong system needs the doctor who treats the case and the system that prevents the next outbreak.

Prevention is hard to fund because success looks like nothing happening. The cliff parable shows the pattern: budgets go to the ambulance at the bottom, while the fence at the top is cheaper per case. **The further upstream you act, the more people you protect.** Immunisation, water and sanitation, tobacco tax and salt reduction are the standard best buys.

left.title: Clinical care
items: Success is a patient who recovers

right.title: Public health
items: Success is fewer people falling ill

key_terms.meaning: Preventing disease and promoting health through the organised efforts of society.
Health outcomes of a group and how they are distributed within it.
Acting on causes such as water, fuel and policy before illness.
Assessment, policy, assurance, promotion and equity.
An intervention with very low cost per DALY averted.
Ensuring services, a competent workforce and access exist.

worked_example.title: Place each action on the stream
worked_example.setup: A district health officer lists four actions for diarrhoea. Decide which are downstream and which upstream, using the deck's examples.
steps: Prescribing ORS and antibiotics: downstream, treating the case.
Rehydrating a dehydrated child: downstream.
Piped water and sanitation: upstream, stopping exposure.
Rotavirus vaccine in the schedule: upstream, protecting the host.
Handwashing promotion is also upstream and usually cheaper per case averted.
worked_example.answer: ORS and rehydration are downstream; water, sanitation, vaccine and handwashing are upstream, cheaper per case and harder to fund.

mistakes: Treating public health as advice to individuals, which gives away most of its leverage.
Counting a sanctioned post as capacity when nobody fills it.
Funding surveillance that reports into a database no one reads.
Importing a cost-effectiveness ranking without checking local burden.

recall.q: What is the unit of concern in public health?
recall.a: The group: villages, districts and nations, not the individual patient.

recall.q: Which word in the WHO definition is contested, and why?
recall.a: "Complete", because nobody is ever completely well, which makes health unattainable.

recall.q: Name the five core functions.
recall.a: Assessment, policy, assurance, promotion and equity.

recall.q: Why does prevention struggle for funding?
recall.a: Its success is invisible, attribution is almost impossible, and a programme that works completely looks unnecessary.

recall.q: Name two best buys that need no individual behaviour change.
recall.a: Tobacco taxation and salt reduction in the food supply.

sections.title: Social Determinants of Health
sections.big_idea: Most health is made **outside the clinic**, so health needs policy from every ministry and a focus on gaps that are unfair.
in_plain_words: Where you are born, grow, live, work and age shapes health more than the medicines you take. The Dahlgren and Whitehead rainbow places a person at the centre with layers of influence around them, and only the innermost is fixed. Marmot's work added the gradient: health worsens at every step down the social ladder, even among people with equal healthcare access.

Not every gap is unjust. An inequality is any difference, while an inequity is avoidable and unfair, and it carries an obligation. In South Asia the determinants that bite hardest include sanitation, cooking fuel, caste, gender and air quality. **Treat the causes of the causes**, but stop at the level where you can act.

key_terms.meaning: Non-medical conditions that shape health and gaps between groups.
Health worsening at every step down the social ladder.
A health difference that is avoidable, unfair and unjust.
Universal action, scaled by need.
The upstream condition behind a medical cause, such as no toilet.
Treating roads, water, schools and food as health policy.

worked_example.title: Inequality or inequity?
worked_example.setup: Apply the two-part test from the deck: is the difference avoidable, and is it unfair? Classify four differences.
steps: Older people are frailer than the young: not avoidable and not unjust, so an inequality.
Men and women differ in some conditions: largely biological, so an inequality.
Dalit children are more stunted: avoidable and unfair, so an inequity.
Rural areas have fewer doctors: a policy choice, so an inequity.
Calling a gap an inequity is a normative claim, so state the argument for it.
worked_example.answer: Frailty and sex differences are inequalities; Dalit stunting and rural doctor shortages are inequities.

mistakes: Aiming health promotion only at the lifestyle ring while conditions are set rings further out.
Targeting only the poorest, which leaves most of the burden untouched under a gradient.
Calling a gap inequitable without arguing that it is avoidable and unfair.
Letting "health in all policies" stay a slogan with no impact assessment or cross-ministry body.

recall.q: What did the Whitehall findings overturn?
recall.a: The idea that only absolute deprivation matters, and that access to care explains the gap.

recall.q: What is the practical answer Marmot proposes?
recall.a: Proportionate universalism: universal action scaled by need.

recall.q: Name three determinants that bite hardest in South Asia.
recall.a: Any three of: sanitation, clean cooking fuel, caste and tribe, gender, air quality, income and informality.

recall.q: Where does the cause-of-the-cause ladder start and end?
recall.a: Outcome, cause, cause of the cause, then root: poverty, exclusion and weak governance.

recall.q: Give one non-health policy that affects health, with its effect.
recall.a: A transport ministry setting speed limits reduces injury deaths more than a trauma programme.

sections.title: Epidemiology Basics
sections.big_idea: Epidemiology counts disease by **person, place and time**, and the incidence and prevalence pair is tied together by duration.
in_plain_words: Epidemiology answers who, where and when, then why and how. Descriptive work is enough for most operational decisions, and skipping it is how outbreak investigations settle on the wrong source. Learn the vocabulary of proportion, ratio and rate, and always ask for the denominator.

Incidence counts new cases, which measures risk. Prevalence counts all existing cases, which measures burden. A long-lasting disease such as diabetes has high prevalence with modest incidence. **Prevalence is roughly incidence multiplied by duration**, so a better treatment can raise prevalence while lowering deaths. Study design then decides what you can claim about cause.

diagram.note: plan services with prevalence, judge prevention with incidence

key_terms.meaning: New cases arising over a period among people at risk.
All existing cases in a population at a point in time.
Events per population per unit of time.
New infections caused by one case in a fully susceptible population.
Cases plotted over time; its shape hints at the source.
Compares sick and well people, looking back at exposure.

worked_example.title: Incidence, prevalence and duration
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a town of 10,000 people at risk of a chronic disease. In one year 50 new cases arise. Each case lasts about 8 years.
steps: As a yearly proportion: 50 ÷ 10,000 = 0.005.
Prevalence is roughly incidence times duration: 0.005 × 8 = 0.04.
So about 4 per cent of the town has the disease at any moment.
A better treatment that adds years of life raises the duration and so the prevalence.
worked_example.answer: Incidence is 500 per 100,000 a year and prevalence about 4 per cent, which rises if people live longer with the disease.

mistakes: Reading a rise in prevalence as a worsening epidemic when treatment is keeping people alive.
Comparing raw counts across populations instead of rates with a stated denominator.
Jumping to a cause before describing the cases by person, place and time.
Using a loose case definition that swamps the outbreak signal.

recall.q: Which measure fits the question "is the programme preventing new cases?"
recall.a: Incidence.

recall.q: What does R0 above 1 mean?
recall.a: Each case causes more than one new infection, so the epidemic grows.

recall.q: What does a single sharp peak on an epidemic curve suggest?
recall.a: A point source.

recall.q: What are the three corners of the epidemiological triad?
recall.a: Agent, host and environment.

recall.q: Which study design is strongest for causation?
recall.a: A randomised trial.

sections.title: Measuring Population Health
sections.big_idea: Count deaths, illness and healthy years, and treat the numbers as **estimates with known gaps**, never as exact counts.
in_plain_words: Vital statistics are the dashboard of public health: mortality, morbidity and survival. Each Indian source has a known gap. Registration is uneven, sample systems lag by years, most deaths are uncertified, and facility data are biased towards what is monitored. That is why disease-burden estimates carry wide intervals.

Mortality indicators use different bases: IMR and U5MR per 1,000 births, MMR per 100,000. Mortality alone misses people living with illness, so the DALY adds years of life lost to early death and years lived with disability. **Use DALYs and hold the critique**, because their weights are contested values. Surveillance turns data into action.

diagram.caption: four ways of counting a population's health

key_terms.meaning: Infant deaths under 1 year per 1,000 live births.
Maternal deaths per 100,000 live births.
One lost year of healthy life, adding YLL and YLD.
Years of life lost to early death against a reference life expectancy.
Years lived with disability: duration times disability weight.
Ongoing collection and use of health data to act early.

worked_example.title: Count deaths and DALYs
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a district has 2,000 live births in a year and an infant mortality rate of 27 per 1,000. A person who dies at 60 is compared with a reference life expectancy of 70, and lived 10 years with a condition of disability weight 0.2.
steps: Neonatal share of infant deaths, using 20 of 27: 20 ÷ 27 = 74%.
YLL for the person who dies at 60: 70 − 60 = 10.
worked_example.answer: 54 infant deaths, about 74 per cent of them neonatal, and a DALY total of 12 for the person in the example.

mistakes: Mixing the bases of IMR and MMR, which differ by a factor of 100.
Quoting cause-of-death figures as counts, when most deaths are uncertified.
Presenting a DALY as a neutral measurement.
Treating HMIS facility figures as coverage without triangulating against surveys.

recall.q: What does neonatal mortality now make up of infant deaths in India?
recall.a: The majority of them.

recall.q: What two parts make a DALY?
recall.a: Years of life lost to early death and years lived with disability.

recall.q: Why are disease-burden estimates revised between rounds?
recall.a: Most deaths are uncertified, so estimates rest on verbal autopsy and modelling with wide intervals.

recall.q: Which Indian system collects births and deaths by sampling, and what is its gap?
recall.a: The Sample Registration System, which lags by years.

recall.q: When is surveillance worth its cost?
recall.a: When it triggers action rather than reporting into a database nobody reads.

sections.title: Communicable Disease & Immunisation
sections.big_idea: Infection travels along a **chain of six links**, and breaking the cheapest link prevents the disease.
in_plain_words: The chain of infection runs from agent to reservoir, portal of exit, transmission, portal of entry and a susceptible host. Prevention means breaking any one link. Transmission is usually the cheapest to break at population scale and the host the most durable, which is why sanitation and vaccination are the two great interventions.

Vaccines train immunity in advance, and herd immunity protects those who cannot be vaccinated once a threshold is passed. The threshold rises with R0, so measles needs about 95 per cent coverage. India's UIP shows the last-mile lesson: the final coverage points cost far more per child. **National averages hide clusters** of unvaccinated children, which is where outbreaks start.

diagram.caption: break any one link and transmission stops

key_terms.meaning: The links from pathogen to susceptible host.
Enough immunity that a pathogen cannot find new hosts.
The temperature-controlled path vaccines need until use.
Universal Immunisation Programme, free vaccines against a dozen-plus diseases.
Drive to reach children the routine programme misses.
Antimicrobial resistance, bacteria that antibiotics no longer kill.

worked_example.title: How far is a block from herd immunity?
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a block has 1,000 children and the measles threshold in the deck is about 95 per cent. The block average is 90 per cent, but one village of 100 children has 60 per cent covered.
steps: Immune children needed in the block: 1,000 × 95 ÷ 100 = 950.
Immune children at 90 per cent: 1,000 × 90 ÷ 100 = 900.
Shortfall for the block: 950 − 900 = 50.
Immune children in the village at 60 per cent: 100 × 60 ÷ 100 = 60.
Gap in that village alone: 95 − 60 = 35 children short of the threshold.
worked_example.answer: The block is 50 children short, and one village is 35 children short of 95, so an average of 90 per cent hides where outbreaks will start.

mistakes: Using one national coverage figure when unvaccinated children cluster by geography and community.
Treating a vaccine that blocks only severe disease as one that gives herd immunity.
Counting toilets built without checking use, which ends the barrier on paper.
Funding TB programmes without a way to notify private-sector cases.

recall.q: Which link does sanitation break and which does a vaccine protect?
recall.a: Sanitation breaks transmission and a vaccine protects the susceptible host.

recall.q: Why does measles return first when immunisation slips?
recall.a: Its high R0 demands one of the highest immunity thresholds, around 95 per cent.

recall.q: What was the lesson of India's polio-free certification in 2014?
recall.a: The campaign was designed around the last mile, where the final coverage points cost far more per child.

recall.q: What is the central operational problem for TB control in India?
recall.a: Private-sector cases going unnotified.

recall.q: Why is AMR a One Health problem?
recall.a: It is generated across humans, animals and the environment at once, so acting in one domain alone does not contain it.

sections.title: Non-Communicable Diseases
sections.big_idea: South Asia carries a **double burden**, with NCDs rising before infection and undernutrition are beaten, and policy is the main lever.
in_plain_words: The epidemiological transition moves the main burden from infection and child deaths to chronic disease. South Asia's version is not sequential: NCDs rose before the old agenda was resolved, so systems run both on one budget. The double burden even appears inside one household, with a stunted child and a diabetic parent.

Four diseases share a small set of modifiable risk factors: tobacco, unhealthy diet, inactivity, alcohol and air pollution. Every lever is regulatory, which is why WHO's best buys centre on tax, labelling and reformulation. **Mental health and injuries** belong in the picture and are chronically under-funded. Tobacco tax is the most effective NCD measure and meets the most lobbying.

key_terms.meaning: The shift of main burden from infections to chronic disease.
Infectious disease and NCDs, or under- and overnutrition, together.
Change from traditional diets to processed food and less activity.
A cause of NCDs that policy can change.
Trained non-specialists delivering mental health care.
Limiting access to lethal methods, such as some pesticides.

worked_example.title: Match each risk factor to its lever
worked_example.setup: A state health secretary asks which population-level lever answers each risk factor in the deck.
steps: Tobacco, including smokeless: tax, plain packaging and smoke-free spaces.
Salt, sugar and trans-fat: reformulation, labelling and trans-fat limits.
Physical inactivity: walkable streets and public transport.
Harmful alcohol: tax, availability and advertising limits.
Air pollution: emission standards and clean cooking fuel.
worked_example.answer: Each risk factor has a regulatory lever: taxes, labels, street design, limits and emission standards, with advice a minor supplement.

mistakes: Designing tobacco control around cigarettes and missing gutka and khaini.
Applying BMI thresholds imported unadjusted, which under-detect risk in South Asians.
Trying to close the mental health gap with specialists alone.
Leaving injuries out of health planning even though they strike the working years.

recall.q: Why is South Asia's transition not the textbook sequence?
recall.a: NCDs rose before communicable disease and undernutrition were resolved.

recall.q: Name the five risk factors that drive most NCDs.
recall.a: Tobacco, unhealthy diet, physical inactivity, harmful alcohol use and air pollution.

recall.q: Which route to closing the mental health treatment gap has evidence behind it?
recall.a: Task-sharing with trained non-specialists.

recall.q: What is among the best-evidenced suicide prevention measures in South Asia?
recall.a: Pesticide regulation that restricts the most lethal compounds.

recall.q: What is the obstacle to the WHO best buys?
recall.a: Rarely evidence or cost, and usually industry opposition.

sections.title: Maternal, Newborn, Child Health & Nutrition
sections.big_idea: Care must connect across a **continuum**, and the remedies for mothers and newborns are old, cheap and depend on trained hands.
in_plain_words: Maternal and child health is a continuum from adolescence to early childhood. India has largely closed the childbirth link, at about 89 per cent institutional, and left the stages either side weakest. The three delays (deciding, reaching, receiving care) are the main diagnostic for maternal death, and as facility births rise the third delay binds.

Newborn care needs no electricity or specialist: warmth, early breastfeeding, a clean cord and resuscitation. Nutrition is set in the first 1,000 days, and stunting is largely irreversible after two. **Food alone never fixes stunting**, because repeated infection drains nutrients, so water and sanitation are nutrition inputs. ICDS and POSHAN have the right design and fall short on workload and supervision.

diagram.caption: the first 1,000 days, and the window that closes

key_terms.meaning: Linked stages of care from adolescence through early childhood.
Delay in deciding, reaching and receiving care.
Home-based newborn care visits by an ASHA after birth.
Low height-for-age, a sign of chronic undernutrition.
Low weight-for-height, acute and dangerous.
Anganwadi-based child nutrition services and the mission around them.

worked_example.title: Read the NFHS nutrition table
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's figures for children under five: stunting 29.3 per cent in NFHS-6 and 35.5 in NFHS-5; wasting 19.0 and 19.3.
steps: Fall in stunting: 35.5 − 29.3 = 6.2 percentage points.
As a share of the earlier level: 6.2 ÷ 35.5 = 17.5%.
Fall in wasting: 19.3 − 19.0 = 0.3 percentage points.
Wasting barely moved, which fits the slide's point that supplementary feeding alone has not shifted it.
worked_example.answer: Stunting fell 6.2 points, about 17.5 per cent in relative terms, while wasting fell only 0.3 points.

mistakes: Treating high institutional delivery as the end of maternal care when postnatal contact and anaemia are the weak stages.
Using feeding programmes alone to fix stunting while infection continues.
Adding duties to ICDS workers without addressing workload, supply and supervision.
Reaching school-age children to address stunting, which is largely set before age two.

recall.q: What are the three delays?
recall.a: Delay in deciding to seek care, in reaching a facility, and in receiving adequate care there.

recall.q: Name three newborn interventions that need no electricity or specialist.
recall.a: Any three of: kangaroo mother care, bag-and-mask resuscitation, early breastfeeding, clean cord care, home visits.

recall.q: What does the HBNC schedule leave uncovered?
recall.a: Days one and two after birth, once early discharge is the norm.

recall.q: Which indicator is the emergency one and which the developmental one?
recall.a: Wasting is the emergency indicator; stunting is the developmental one.

recall.q: Which ICDS component has the strongest evidence and is least delivered?
recall.a: Behaviour-change counselling for mothers.

sections.title: Health Systems
sections.big_idea: A health system is **six building blocks** where readiness is a conjunction, so the weakest block sets the capability.
in_plain_words: A health system is every organisation, person and action whose main purpose is health: hospitals and also financing, workforce, supplies, information and governance. WHO's six building blocks are a diagnostic frame that stops an assessment becoming a facility count. Five strong blocks and one weak gives you the capability of the weak one.

Financing decides equity. Out-of-pocket payment charges people when they are least able to earn, while tax-funded and pooled schemes protect. Universal Health Coverage means needed services, of adequate quality, without financial hardship, for everyone. **The quality clause is the one most often dropped.** Primary health care, from Alma-Ata to Astana, is the foundation, and its political parts were the first to be narrowed.

key_terms.meaning: WHO's six parts of a health system.
The patient paying at the point of care.
Needed quality services for all without financial hardship.
Three axes: who is covered, which services, what share of cost.
1978 declaration making primary health care the foundation.
A short list of vertical interventions that narrowed Alma-Ata.

worked_example.title: Why averaging a scorecard misleads
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a district scores each of the six building blocks from 1 to 5. Five blocks score 5 and medical products score 2. Financing shares from the 2021-22 accounts are also on the slide: out-of-pocket 39.4 per cent, government 48.
steps: Sum of scores: 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 2 = 27.
Average score: 27 ÷ 6 = 4.5, which looks excellent.
Readiness is a conjunction, so the capability is the weakest block: 2.
Financing: 39.4 + 48 = 87.4 per cent from these two sources.
The remaining share of spending: 100 − 87.4 = 12.6.
worked_example.answer: The average is 4.5 but the real capability is 2, set by the weak block, and out-of-pocket plus government spending account for 87.4 per cent.

mistakes: Assessing a health system by counting facilities.
Producing doctors and expecting rural posts to fill without addressing housing, schooling and isolation.
Extending services first, which tends to benefit those already covered.
Treating Astana as a change in itself, when it depends on financing.

recall.q: Name the six WHO building blocks.
recall.a: Service delivery, health workforce, information, medical products and vaccines, financing, and leadership and governance.

recall.q: Why is out-of-pocket payment the most regressive way to finance health?
recall.a: It charges people precisely when they are least able to earn.

recall.q: What are the three dimensions of moving towards UHC?
recall.a: Who is covered, which services, and what share of cost is covered.

recall.q: Which Alma-Ata principles were dropped?
recall.a: Community control over services and action outside the health sector.

recall.q: Why does contribution-based insurance struggle in South Asia?
recall.a: Most workers are informal, with no payroll to deduct from.

sections.title: India's Health System
sections.big_idea: India's system is **federal and mixed**: states vary enormously, the private sector delivers much care, and low public spending leaves families paying.
in_plain_words: Health is mainly a state subject, so the centre sets policy and co-funds while states run services. National averages therefore describe no state. The rural public structure is a pyramid from sub-centre or HWC to PHC, CHC and district hospital, and specialist vacancies at the CHC are the structural bottleneck.

The National Health Mission's lasting gift is institutional: the ASHA cadre, untied funds and data systems. Ayushman Bharat has two pillars, HWCs for primary care and PM-JAY for hospital cover. Most out-of-pocket spending is outpatient, which PM-JAY leaves out, so **HWC implementation is the more consequential half**. Low public spending and high out-of-pocket payment are one fact seen twice.

diagram.caption: routine care low, complex care up

key_terms.meaning: A matter where states run services and the centre sets policy.
National Health Mission, launched in 2005 as the National Rural Health Mission.
Accredited Social Health Activist, a local woman linking homes to services.
Health and Wellness Centre, an upgraded sub-centre or PHC.
Ayushman Bharat's hospital insurance cover for poor families.
Facility-level management and grievance body.

worked_example.title: How many facilities would a block need?
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a block of 100,000 people. Use the deck's indicative norms, which differ for tribal and hilly areas.
steps: Sub-Centres at 5,000 people each: 100,000 ÷ 5,000 = 20.
Sub-Centres at 3,000 people each: 100,000 ÷ 3,000 = 33.33.
Primary Health Centres at 30,000 each: 100,000 ÷ 30,000 = 3.33.
Primary Health Centres at 20,000 each: 100,000 ÷ 20,000 = 5.
A hilly block would need more, since norms count people and not travel time.
worked_example.answer: About 20 to 33 sub-centres and 3 to 5 PHCs, with a hilly block needing more because norms ignore travel time.

mistakes: Quoting a national average when state variation is the key fact.
Counting sanctioned CHC posts as capacity when the specialist post is vacant.
Adding duties for ASHAs without payment, which makes pilots fail at scale.
Reading PM-JAY as covering outpatient care and medicines.

recall.q: Who runs most health services in India?
recall.a: States, because health is mainly a state subject.

recall.q: What is the structural bottleneck at CHC level?
recall.a: Specialist vacancies, so complications are referred on to the district hospital.

recall.q: What does the ASHA incentive list function as?
recall.a: The job description, so unpaid tasks such as postnatal counselling lapse first.

recall.q: What do the two Ayushman Bharat pillars cover?
recall.a: HWCs cover comprehensive primary care; PM-JAY covers secondary and tertiary hospitalisation.

recall.q: What did NHP 2017 aim for in public spending?
recall.a: A goal of raising it toward 2.5 per cent of GDP.

sections.title: Health Equity & Global Health
sections.big_idea: Care follows the **inverse care law**, so look at who is left out locally, and treat pandemics, climate and global health as shared problems.
in_plain_words: Julian Tudor Hart's inverse care law says good medical care varies inversely with need. It works through where facilities are, who can reach them, how people are treated on arrival and what is in stock. A universal programme delivered without extra effort for the hardest to reach widens gaps, since the advantaged take it up first. Always disaggregate: disaggregating data you already hold costs nothing.

Health also crosses borders and sectors. The IHR bind countries to report, but prompt reporters face restrictions. One Health links people, animals and environment, and most new epidemics are zoonotic. Climate change hits the poorest first through heat, vectors, weather and crop failure. **Climate action brings immediate local health gains**, which makes health the more persuasive frame.

diagram.caption: equity at home, and shared risk across borders

key_terms.meaning: Good medical care varies inversely with the need for it.
Reporting results by caste, sex, disability, distance and so on.
Rules binding countries to detect, report and respond to health emergencies.
Linking human, animal and environmental health.
A disease that jumps from animals to people.
A health gain that comes from climate action.

worked_example.title: An average that hides a gap
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a district has 1,000 households, of which 200 are in Dalit hamlets. A programme reaches 80 per cent of other households and 56 per cent of Dalit households.
steps: Other households reached: 800 × 80 ÷ 100 = 640.
Dalit households reached: 200 × 56 ÷ 100 = 112.
Total reached: 640 + 112 = 752.
District average: 752 ÷ 1,000 = 75.2%.
The gap between groups: 80 − 56 = 24 points, which the average conceals.
worked_example.answer: The district reads 75.2 per cent while Dalit households are 24 points behind, so only disaggregation shows the failure.

mistakes: Assuming that removing the fee removes the inverse care law.
Reporting a good national average and stopping there.
Building human-only surveillance, which detects outbreaks after they cross into people.
Presenting climate action as a global, distant benefit when the local health gain is the stronger case.

recall.q: Through what four routes does the inverse care law operate?
recall.a: Facility location, who can reach them, treatment on arrival, and what is available when they get there.

recall.q: What is the structural flaw in the IHR reporting system?
recall.a: A country that reports promptly faces trade and travel restrictions, a penalty for compliance.

recall.q: Which group is the most invisible in Indian health data?
recall.a: Urban slum populations.

recall.q: Why is health a persuasive frame for climate policy?
recall.a: The health co-benefits arrive locally and immediately while the climate benefit is global and delayed.

recall.q: How was smallpox eradicated?
recall.a: Through surveillance and ring vaccination, with global cooperation.

sections.title: Prevention in Practice & Further Reading
sections.big_idea: Ask **at which level** a programme acts and whether it could act one level earlier, then judge it by who it reaches.
in_plain_words: Prevention has four levels: primordial, primary, secondary and tertiary. The earlier you act, the more people you protect at lower cost per person, yet budgets run in almost the reverse order. Primordial prevention is the level most often omitted. Screening needs a recall and treatment pathway, or it finds people and loses them.

Geoffrey Rose showed that most cases arise in the large group at modest risk, so a population strategy beats treating only the high-risk few, though each person gains little. Health promotion in the Ottawa Charter is five actions and only one is communication. In a crisis, **speed matters more than polish**. Start your own reading with the NFHS district fact sheets.

diagram.caption: reach falls and cost per person rises along the line

key_terms.meaning: Stopping risk factors from arising, such as clean air policy.
Catching disease early, for example by screening.
A measure with large population benefit gives each person little.
Shifting the whole distribution of risk.
Enabling people to increase control over their health, per the Ottawa Charter.
Honest, trusted, two-way communication during a health threat.

worked_example.title: High-risk or population strategy?
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a population of 10,000 splits into 1,000 people at high risk, where 5 per cent develop the disease, and 9,000 at modest risk, where 1 per cent do.
steps: Cases in the high-risk group: 1,000 × 5 ÷ 100 = 50.
Cases in the modest-risk group: 9,000 × 1 ÷ 100 = 90.
Total cases: 50 + 90 = 140.
Share from the modest-risk group: 90 ÷ 140 = 64.3%.
Treating only the high-risk group leaves 90 of 140 cases untouched.
worked_example.answer: About 64 per cent of cases arise in the modest-risk group, which is why Rose argued for a population strategy.

mistakes: Screening with no recall and treatment pathway, which finds disease and loses people.
Reducing health promotion to poster campaigns and messaging.
Lecturing people to change when the shop sells only junk and wages buy the cheapest calories.
Changing guidance without explaining the reasoning, which damages trust.

recall.q: Who added the primordial level and when?
recall.a: Strasser, in 1978, to Leavell and Clark's three levels.

recall.q: What is Rose's prevention paradox?
recall.a: A measure that brings large benefit to a population often offers little to each individual.

recall.q: What are the Ottawa Charter's five actions?
recall.a: Enabling people, healthy public policy, supportive environments, community action and reorienting health services.

recall.q: Name two risk communication principles.
recall.a: Any two of: make the healthy choice the easy choice, use trusted local messengers, be honest about uncertainty, fill the vacuum early, address stigma.

recall.q: Which item in the reading list is most immediately usable for your district?
recall.a: The NFHS district fact sheets.

notes.2: Read the agenda as an arc from ideas to measures to systems. Sections 1 to 3 give the concepts, section 4 the numbers, sections 5 to 7 the major health areas, sections 8 and 9 the systems, and sections 10 and 11 equity and action. **Start with the section that matches your work.**
notes.4: Learn the WHO definition and its critique together. The phrase to hold is "not merely the absence of disease", which changed policy. The contested word is **complete**, since nobody is ever completely well. Then switch units: a clinician asks about this patient and public health asks about the next thousand.
notes.5: Memorise the two definitions and the phrase **organised efforts of society**. It puts law, infrastructure, collective financing and surveillance at the centre and treats advice to individuals as a small part. Framing public health as behaviour change gives away most of its leverage.
notes.6: Use the two tables to explain why public health is underfunded: success looks like nothing happening. A hospital that saves a life produces a story, while an outbreak prevented produces nothing to point at. A programme that works completely **looks unnecessary**, so its budget gets cut.
notes.7: Remember the parable in four steps: ambulance, early detection, fence, moving the path. The slide's argument is about proportion, since budgets go overwhelmingly to the ambulance. The sharpest question is the last: **why does the only road to the market run along the edge?**
notes.8: Place any action on the stream: downstream treats the case, upstream stops it. Upstream protects more people and is usually cheaper per case, yet it is harder to fund because the benefit is spread out and belongs to no single ministry. **Both are needed, and only one is usually built.**
notes.9: Learn five functions: assessment, policy, assurance, promotion, equity. Then use the weak-when column as a diagnostic. Assurance fails quietly, because **a sanctioned post with nobody in it** still counts as capacity in every plan. Assessment without action is the other common failure.
notes.10: The best buys are childhood immunisation, water and sanitation, tobacco tax and salt reduction. The last two need nobody to change behaviour, so they last. Remember the caution: **cost-effectiveness depends on setting**, and bed nets are a poor buy where malaria is absent.
notes.12: The big insight is that most of health is made outside the clinic. Use the table to trace how each determinant reaches the body. Estimates of the clinic's share vary, but every one puts medical care in the minority, which is the argument for **health in all policies**.
notes.13: Picture five layers around a person, with only the innermost fixed. Each outer layer is something policy can change. The warning on the slide: health promotion aimed at the lifestyle ring **puts responsibility on individuals** for conditions set rings further out.
notes.14: Two children born the same day in the same city can differ by years in life expectancy, and none of the differences in the table is genetic. Use the rows as a checklist: water, sanitation, cooking fuel, school. **The gap is produced by decisions**, so decisions can close it.
notes.15: Marmot's finding is a gradient: health worsens at every step down the ladder, even among employed, housed people with health cover. So targeting only the poorest leaves most of the burden. His answer is **proportionate universalism**, universal action scaled by need.
notes.16: Apply the two-part test: avoidable and unfair means inequity. Older people being frailer is an inequality, while Dalit children being more stunted is an inequity. Calling a gap inequitable is a **normative claim**, so argue it. It also creates an obligation, because someone is responsible.
notes.17: Use this table as a shortlist of determinants to look for first. The sanitation row carries a lesson: **benefit follows use**, so counting toilets built overstates the effect. Air quality has moved from a Delhi-winter story to a year-round national one.
notes.18: Walk down the ladder from outcome to root and notice that each step up is cheaper per case but harder to act on. Stop at the level where you can act. Poverty is the root, but for a district health officer **the toilet and the pipe are actionable**.
notes.19: Health in all policies means roads, water, schools, food and housing are health policy. A transport ministry setting speed limits can do more for injury deaths than a trauma programme. Without a **health impact assessment or cross-ministry body**, the phrase is a slogan.
notes.21: Epidemiology answers who, where and when, then why. Descriptive work on person, place and time is enough for most operational decisions. The common slip is hurry: jumping to a cause before describing the distribution is **how outbreak investigations settle on the wrong source**.
notes.22: Use the sink picture: incidence is the speed of the tap and prevalence is the water in the sink. Remember the link: **prevalence is roughly incidence multiplied by duration**. A better treatment raises prevalence while lowering deaths, so a rise is not always a worse epidemic.
notes.23: Match the question to the measure. How fast is it spreading, or is prevention working? Incidence. How many need treatment or beds now? Prevalence. Using one for the other gives wrong budgets and wrong conclusions. For chronic disease such as diabetes, **the stock is huge while the annual flow is small**.
notes.24: Always demand the denominator. A proportion has its numerator inside the whole, a ratio compares two separate quantities, and a rate counts events over time. Only a rate compares populations of different sizes. The **maternal mortality ratio** is a ratio because it divides by live births.
notes.25: Learn the triangle of agent, host and environment, and three ways to break it: kill the agent, protect the host, change the environment. The environment tends to be most durable, since a drained breeding site works without anyone remembering. The triad fits infections and **does not carry over to NCDs**.
notes.26: Memorise the five steps and the slip at each. The case definition is the decision everything rests on: too broad swamps the signal, too narrow misses the outbreak. Learn to read the curve: **one sharp peak means a point source**, a long plateau means continuing exposure.
notes.27: The threshold at 1 is the idea: above 1 the epidemic grows, below 1 it dies out. The values in the table are approximate. Measles needs about 95 per cent coverage, so it returns first when immunisation slips. R0 depends on contacts and density, so it is **not a fixed property of a germ**.
notes.28: Match design to question. A cross-sectional snapshot gives prevalence, case-control suits rare disease, cohorts give incidence and risk, and trials give the strongest causal claim. Know each weakness in the second table. The **Bradford Hill considerations** help judge whether an association is causal.
notes.30: Count first. Use the table to see where each statistic comes from and where it fails: registration is uneven, sample systems lag, and most deaths are uncertified. Treat disease-burden figures as **estimates with wide intervals**, and quote them that way.
notes.31: Learn the indicators with their denominators: IMR, U5MR and NMR per 1,000 live births, MMR per 100,000. Neonatal deaths now form most infant deaths, around 20 of 27, so **gains lie in the first 28 days**. Check the current SRS bulletin and the state spread before quoting.
notes.32: This chart makes one point: infant and under-five mortality have fallen sharply over three decades. The slide says the plotted values are rounded and illustrative, so quote the direction and take numbers from the SRS. It is **a major success still in progress**.
notes.33: Maternal mortality has more than halved this century, while state gaps remain wide, with southern states far ahead of several northern ones. As on the last chart, the values are rounded for teaching. When you present it, **show the state spread** beside the national line.
notes.34: Mortality tells who dies and misses everyone living with illness. As people live longer, depression, back pain and vision loss cause large burden with almost no deaths. DALYs give non-fatal conditions **a place in the budget argument**, though their weights are contested.
notes.35: Life expectancy at birth is a single summary: the average years a newborn would live if current death rates held. The slide says it has roughly doubled since Independence to about 70, and the chart values are rounded. It is **still below the global frontier**.
notes.36: Deaths and burden give different lists. Heart disease tops mortality, while depression and back pain top disability burden. The list you plan from decides whether mental health and musculoskeletal conditions get any resources. Deaths in the young count for more DALYs, **a deliberate value choice**.
notes.37: A DALY is years of life lost plus years lived with disability. YLD is duration times disability weight, and YLL compares age at death with a reference life expectancy. Use DALYs and keep the critique: **weights come from surveys, not people living with the condition**.
notes.38: Surveillance is information for action. Know the four Indian systems and their limits: IDSP depends on reporting discipline, HMIS counts services and not outcomes, SRS lags, CRS is incomplete on cause. What is monitored gets recorded generously, so **triangulate with survey data**.
notes.40: Learn the chain: agent, reservoir, portal of exit, transmission, portal of entry and host. Prevention means breaking any one link, so pick the cheapest. Transmission is usually cheapest at population scale and the host the most durable, which is why **sanitation and vaccination** are the two great interventions.
notes.41: Match each route to its barrier. Airborne by ventilation and vaccines, faecal-oral by water and sanitation, vector-borne by nets and source control, blood by safe injections, contact by hygiene. **The failure column is where programmes break**, such as toilets built and unused.
notes.42: Know the four vaccine types and the constraint they share: the cold chain, where programmes in hot, remote districts actually fail. Persuasion is a smaller problem. Complacency is the other risk, as **coverage falls once a disease becomes rare** enough to seem unimportant.
notes.43: Herd immunity needs a threshold that rises with R0, about 95 per cent for measles. Two cautions: coverage must be measured locally, since national averages hide pockets, and **a vaccine that only prevents severe disease** does not generate herd immunity.
notes.44: The UIP gives free vaccines against a dozen-plus diseases, and Mission Indradhanush targets missed children. Polio-free certification in 2014 came from a campaign built around the last mile. The lesson: the final coverage points cost far more per child, so **average-cost budgets will not reach them**.
notes.45: Full immunisation among children aged 12 to 23 months has risen markedly across NFHS rounds, though the chart values are rounded for teaching. Pair the trend with the slide's warning that the unreached child is the hardest, and **where herd immunity is won or lost**.
notes.46: Three diseases, three programmes: NTEP for TB, NACO for HIV, NVBDCP for malaria. The tools exist, so the challenge is reach, adherence and stigma. For TB the central problem is private-sector cases going unnotified, and **incomplete treatment later becomes drug resistance**.
notes.47: AMR is a slow-motion crisis driven by misuse in people, animals and hospitals. Link each driver to its response in the table. The animal row sits with agriculture ministries, out of reach of health programmes, which makes AMR **the clearest case for One Health**.
notes.49: The transition moves the main burden from infections and child deaths to chronic disease. South Asia sits in the double burden stage, with both at once. The textbook order is sequential, but NCDs rose before the old agenda was resolved, so **one budget must run both agendas**.
notes.50: The chart is labelled illustrative of a well-established transition: the NCD share of deaths rises while infection is still present. The point to take away is the strain on systems built for the old battle. Use it with the stage table and **take figures from WHO or GBD**.
notes.51: Diets and bodies are changing together: processed food is cheaper, salt, sugar and trans-fat sit in the supply, activity falls, and undernutrition persists. South Asians develop diabetes at lower BMI, so imported thresholds under-detect risk. **Regulating the food supply reaches everyone.**
notes.52: Four diseases share a small set of modifiable risk factors, which makes prevention possible. Note the South Asian particularities: heart disease strikes roughly a decade earlier, diabetes at lower BMI, and tobacco-linked oral cancer is prominent. Earlier onset means NCDs hit **working years** and cost more income.
notes.53: Five risk factors drive most NCDs, and every lever listed is regulatory: tax, packaging, reformulation, walkable streets, emission standards. They are modifiable by policy and only marginally by advice. **Smokeless tobacco** such as gutka and khaini matters most here and gets least attention.
notes.54: Mental health is public health. The treatment gap is the central fact, and specialists cannot close it because there are too few psychiatrists. **Task-sharing with trained non-specialists** is the route with evidence. The Mental Healthcare Act 2017 is rights-based, though implementation lags behind it.
notes.55: Injuries kill and disable the young and working-age, so their DALY burden is large. The proven interventions are engineering and law: helmets, speed limits, barriers, clean fuel. **Pesticide regulation** is among the best-evidenced suicide prevention measures, because many attempts are impulsive and method-dependent.
notes.56: Learn the five best buys and why they qualify: they are cost-effective, population-wide and mostly regulatory. Tobacco taxation is the most effective NCD intervention and one of few that raises revenue. The obstacle is rarely evidence or cost and usually **industry opposition**, which is worth naming.
notes.58: Follow a woman along five stages and ask where she falls out. Childbirth is largely closed, at about 89 per cent institutional, so the weak stages sit on either side. Use the slide's test for any district: of women who delivered in a facility, **how many had a postnatal contact within 48 hours**?
notes.59: Use the three delays as a diagnostic in any maternal death review: deciding, reaching, receiving. Each has a location and a fix. As institutional delivery nears nine in ten, the third delay binds, because remaining deaths are increasingly of **women who did reach a facility**.
notes.60: The proven package is old and cheap: oxytocin, magnesium sulphate, skilled attendance, emergency obstetric care and a postnatal contact. The fourth row is the costly one, and **the anaesthetist is the classic single point of failure**. JSY raised institutional births by paying for them.
notes.61: Newborn deaths are the frontier of child survival, and nothing on the list needs electricity or a specialist. Note the HBNC gap: visits on days 3, 7, 14, 21, 28 and 42 leave **days one and two uncovered** once early discharge is normal.
notes.62: Keep the three indicators distinct: stunting is chronic, wasting is acute and dangerous, underweight mixes both. The table shows stunting at 29.3 per cent in NFHS-6 against 35.5 in NFHS-5. A wasted child needs treatment now, while **a stunted child records damage largely done**.
notes.63: Memorise the window: pregnancy to age two, the first 1,000 days. Growth faltering before two is not recovered by later feeding, so school-age programmes cannot fix stunting. Complementary feeding from six months is the weakest link: diets have energy and **lack diversity**.
notes.64: ICDS and POSHAN offer four services through anganwadis. The design is sound; worker workload, supply and supervision are the constraint. The highest-value component, **counselling for mothers**, is the least delivered because it has no commodity attached and no easy indicator.
notes.65: Food alone never fixes stunting. Repeated enteric infection stops a child absorbing what they eat, so sanitation and clean water are nutrition inputs. This is the deck's clearest case for **cross-sector work**: a nutrition ministry acting without water and sanitation treats one input of several.
notes.67: A health system is more than hospitals: financing, workforce, supplies, information and governance all count. Strengthening it usually means the unglamorous rows. The last row matters most in India, where the **private sector delivers much of the care** and is lightly regulated.
notes.68: Learn the six building blocks and how each fails. The slide's key point is that readiness is a conjunction and not a sum: five strong blocks and one weak gives you the capability of the weak one. So **a scorecard that averages components misleads**.
notes.69: Workforce is a distribution problem as much as a density problem. More doctors do not fill rural posts if housing, schooling, spouse employment and isolation go unaddressed. **Midwifery is the clearest under-investment**, and ASHAs carry the load without a salary.
notes.70: Rank the three ways to pay by equity. Out-of-pocket is worst, because it charges people when they are least able to earn. It was India's largest source until the 2021-22 accounts put it at **39.4 per cent against a government share of 48**. Pooling and prepayment are the way out.
notes.71: UHC means needed services, of adequate quality, without financial hardship, for everyone. The quality clause is the one most often dropped, since coverage figures count contacts. UHC has two indicators, service coverage and catastrophic expenditure, and **a country can improve one while the other worsens**.
notes.72: Picture the cube: who is covered, which services, what share of cost. No country covers everything free, so every system chooses an axis. **Extending the population dimension first** is generally the most equitable route, since extending services first benefits those already covered.
notes.73: Alma-Ata made primary health care the foundation: close to home, community participation, action across sectors. The two dropped principles were the political ones, community control and action outside health. Comprehensive PHC was **narrowed to selective PHC** on grounds of cost, and the argument recurs.
notes.74: Astana 2018 updates the PHC promise for NCDs, ageing and technology, with UHC as the goal. Compare the columns with Alma-Ata. Astana matters as a re-commitment, and whether it changes anything depends on financing, because comprehensive PHC has **lost budget arguments to vertical programmes**.
notes.76: State variation is the single most important fact about Indian health, because health is mainly a state subject. National averages describe no state. A large private sector delivers most outpatient care with light regulation, so **regulating quality, price and notification** matters as much as strengthening public facilities.
notes.77: Learn the pyramid: sub-centre or HWC for 3,000 to 5,000 people, PHC for 20,000 to 30,000, CHC for 80,000 to 120,000, then the district hospital. Specialist vacancies at CHCs are the bottleneck. Norms count people and not travel time, so a hilly sub-centre is **not accessible to most it serves**.
notes.78: NHM's durable contribution is institutional: the ASHA cadre, untied funds, Rogi Kalyan Samitis, free entitlements and flexible state funding. It also created HMIS and name-based tracking, which decided **what can be counted**. Buildings alone would not have changed what states could do.
notes.79: ASHAs are close to a million local women linking households to the health system, paid by incentives. The incentive list works as the job description, so tasks without a payment, such as postnatal counselling, lapse first. Adding a duty means **adding under-paid work to the busiest link**.
notes.80: Ayushman Bharat has two pillars: HWCs for comprehensive primary care and PM-JAY for hospital cover. The gap is that most out-of-pocket spending is outpatient, which PM-JAY leaves out. So the **HWC pillar carries the larger share** of the UHC promise, and PM-JAY depends on private hospitals taking part.
notes.81: Read the four steps as one design: prevention and primary care reduce the need for costly hospital care, while PM-JAY shields families from big bills. One without the other leaves people exposed. Outpatient costs sit outside PM-JAY, so **HWC implementation matters most**.
notes.82: Out-of-pocket spending impoverishes families, because sickness becomes debt. The chart is illustrative, patterned on the National Health Accounts, and shows the share falling but still high. Cutting it is the central UHC challenge. Pair it with the **real 2021-22 figure** of 39.4 per cent from the financing slide.
notes.83: Low public spending and high out-of-pocket payment are the same fact seen twice. Government spending has hovered around 1 to 2 per cent of GDP, with NHP 2017 aiming toward 2.5. **What the state does not fund, households pay for** at the point of illness. Richer-income peers spend more, so it is a choice.
notes.85: Tudor Hart's inverse care law says good care varies inversely with need. It works through facility location, access, treatment on arrival and stockouts, and free systems show it too. The trap: a universal programme without **extra effort for the hardest to reach** widens gaps, because the advantaged take it up first.
notes.86: Always disaggregate. Walk through the groups: caste and tribe, women, remote areas, urban slums, disability, income. Urban slums are the most invisible group in the data, falling between rural norms and urban planning. **Disaggregating data you already hold costs nothing.**
notes.87: The IHR bind countries to detect, report and respond, but the reporting incentive is the structural flaw: prompt reporters face trade and travel restrictions. That **penalty for compliance** explains under-detection. The Pandemic Agreement annex is about making prompt reporting rational and guaranteeing access to countermeasures.
notes.88: One Health links people, animals and environment. Most recent emerging epidemics were zoonotic, so human-only surveillance sees outbreaks after they cross into people, which is already late. Land-use change drives spillover. **AMR is the other One Health problem**, generated across all three domains.
notes.89: Climate change is a health crisis through heat, vector range shifts, extreme weather and crop failure. Heat is the most immediate and measurable pathway for South Asia, and Ahmedabad shows mortality responds to preparation. Every row hits the poorest first, so **untargeted adaptation will widen gaps**.
notes.90: Climate action has local, immediate health co-benefits: clean cooking fuel, fewer vehicle emissions, active transport, greener cities. The benefit is local and quick while the climate gain is global and slow, so **health is the more persuasive frame**. Air-quality rules framed as health measures build coalitions more easily.
notes.91: Global health works through arrangements as much as goodwill. Smallpox eradication in 1980 succeeded through surveillance and ring vaccination, without universal coverage. Gavi, price negotiation and pooled procurement widened access. COVID vaccine distribution is the counter-example: **the technology worked and the allocation did not**.
notes.93: Four levels, and the earlier you act the more people you protect at lower cost per person. Cost rises and reach falls as you move down, yet budgets are allocated in almost the reverse order. Ask of any programme **which level it acts at** and whether it could act one level earlier.
notes.94: Memorise the four with an example each: primordial stops risk factors arising, primary stops disease, secondary catches it early, tertiary limits harm. Primordial is the level most often omitted and has the widest reach. **Screening needs a recall and treatment pathway**, or it finds people and loses them.
notes.95: Rose's insight: most cases arise in the large group at modest risk, so treating only the high-risk few misses most of the burden. This is the prevention paradox. A population measure gives each person a tiny benefit, which is hard to sell by persuasion, so it **works through regulation**.
notes.96: The Ottawa Charter defines health promotion by five actions, and only one is communication. Programmes that reduce it to messaging have adopted the name and dropped the method. Change the environment as well as the message, since **exhortation reaches only those already able to act**.
notes.97: Five communication principles, each preventing a named failure. Speed matters more than polish: an early honest statement that admits what is unknown outperforms a late confident one. Changing guidance damages trust only when the change is unexplained. Use **trusted local messengers** and tackle stigma directly.
notes.98: Start with the NFHS district fact sheets: immunisation, stunting, anaemia, institutional delivery and sanitation for your own district, free to download. Read GBD estimates as **modelled figures with wide intervals**. The other titles give the argument: Marmot for the gradient, Drèze and Sen for India's record.
notes.99: Use the five takeaways as a self-test: can you explain each in a sentence to a colleague? They restate the course: upstream action, social determinants, incidence versus prevalence, primary care as the backbone of UHC, and cutting out-of-pocket spending. **Revisit the section where your answer is weakest.**
